newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU ministers agree detailed EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers agree detailed EMU budget pact.

text.p: European Union finance ministers on Saturday resolved all outstanding differences on a budget accord that would penalise governments running excessive deficits under a single currency.

In a meeting designed to finalise important details of economic and monetary union (EMU) -- set for launch in 1999 -- ministers reached a compromise on whether the fines under a Stability and Growth Pact would be cumulative.
Their agreement, coming amid a period of growing speculation on whether a delay to the single currency's start-date might be needed, gives the project a renewed sense of momentum.
Specifically, the ministers agreed that governments running deficits above three percent of Gross Domestic Product would face a maximum penalty of 0.5 percent of total output per year.

During the first year the fine would include a fixed portion -- 0.2 percent of GDP -- and a variable portion -- an additional 0.1 percent of GDP for every percentage point above the three percent threshold.
Should the offending government fail to bring its finances under control, additional fines, essentially the variable component, would be levied for every year above the target.

While the maximum annual penalty of 0.5 percent of GDP was agreed by EU leaders last December in Dublin, the deal struck on Saturday could in practice mean a much heavier penalty if the deficit lasted for several years.
"This is an application of the Dublin agreement which reinforces the credibility of the Stability and Growth Pact," French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told a news conference.
The ministerial gathering also agreed that only countries within EMU could benefit from the fines collected.

Cheered by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to stand for re-election next year, the ministers, accompanied by central bankers from the 15-nation bloc, are also expected to clarify the timetable for deciding which countries will join EMU.
The preferred time horizon appears to be late-April 1998, a period seen particularly helpful to France which holds parliamentary elections in March next year.
"It's a very reasonable forecast," Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, forerunner to a European Central Bank, told reporters.

After weeks of intense speculation that the 1999 start-date might have to be delayed, Kohl's announcement, coupled with recent upbeat German economic figures, should give the group a chance to reaffirm a timely launch for EMU.
"I think the most important function of this meeting is to confirm once again that this process is on track," Swedish central bank governor Urban Backstrom said.

Uncertainty over Bonn's ability to put its public finances in order in 1997 -- the critical year for those wishing to join the single currency club -- have been primarily behind renewed market speculation that a postponement might be needed.
Budget difficulties have been compounded by record unemployment in Germany and a political backdrop of widening labour unrest and public hostility to a common currency.
But Kohl's decision to stand again gave nearly all the ministers and central bankers renewed confidence in their assessment of the future.
"It is an important decision in favour of the realisation of EMU," Italian Finance Minister Carlo Azaglio Ciampi told reporters during the meeting in this Dutch resort town.
